title: A brain atlas of synapse protein lifetime across the mouse lifespan
abstract: The lifetime of proteins in synapses is important for their signaling, maintenance, and remodeling, and for memory duration. We quantified the lifetime of endogenous PSD95, an abundant postsynaptic protein in excitatory synapses, at single-synapse resolution across the mouse brain and lifespan, generating the Protein Lifetime Synaptome Atlas. Excitatory synapses have a wide range of PSD95 lifetimes extending from hours to several months, with distinct spatial distributions in dendrites, neurons, and brain regions. Synapses with short protein lifetimes are enriched in young animals and in brain regions controlling innate behaviors, whereas synapses with long protein lifetimes accumulate during development, are enriched in the cortex and CA1 where memories are stored, and are preferentially preserved in old age. Synapse protein lifetime increases throughout the brain in a mouse model of autism and schizophrenia. Protein lifetime adds a further layer to synapse diversity and enriches prevailing concepts in brain development, aging, and disease.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This Neuron article has seen clear scholarly uptake, with 122 OpenAlex citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 1% of cited works. Its influence is also visible in downstream reuse and discussion across the neuroscience literature, including substantial preprint circulation and a small but notable set of teaching-adjacent mentions.

Full narrative

A brain atlas of synapse protein lifetime across the mouse lifespan has established itself as a high-impact contribution to synapse biology and systems neuroscience. The study’s central advance is methodological and conceptual: it quantified endogenous PSD95 lifetime at single-synapse resolution across the mouse brain and lifespan, creating a Protein Lifetime Synaptome Atlas that helps explain how synaptic maintenance and remodeling vary across time and space. The citation record reflects that reach, with 122 citations and a top 1% percentile position for its field and publication year.

The article’s uptake is broad but concentrated in neuroscience-adjacent areas that fit its subject matter. Citing works cluster around neuroscience and neuropharmacology, advanced fluorescence microscopy, cellular transport and secretion, neural dynamics, and neurodegeneration-related research, suggesting that the atlas is being used both as a biological reference and as a methodological touchstone. The venue mix also points to visibility in prominent scholarly channels, including bioRxiv, eLife, Scientific Reports, Nature Neuroscience, and Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The record also shows early and sustained dissemination beyond the journal article itself. There are 34 preprint citations among the 122 citing works, indicating that the preprint version was part of the paper’s uptake pathway. In addition, scite reports 9 supporting citation statements, which is consistent with direct scholarly use of the findings rather than only passing mention. Downstream reuse is substantial in aggregate, with 123 documented reuses across articles, preprints, reviews, peer-review content, and one Europe PMC biomedical mention.

Signals of stewardship and adoption are present as well. The work is associated with three funding sources: NIMH NIH HHS, the Swiss National Science Foundation, and the Wellcome Trust. It also carries three RRIDs, which supports reproducibility-oriented use of the resource. Public-facing attention is modest rather than expansive: the digest records one podcast mention and one YouTube-linked teaching use, while other public-discourse fields are unavailable in the current record. Overall, the evidence supports a picture of a methodologically important neuroscience paper with strong academic reach and clear reuse across the synapse and brain-mapping literature.
